1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Basic information: Female patient, 47 years old, chief complaint: "chest tightness after exertion for 1 year, worsening for 3 days." She presented to the Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University, on Day 0, and was transferred to the Fifth Department of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine (Henan Provincial Center for Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Embolism and Pulmonary Hypertension) on Day +6. One year earlier, in approximately 11 months before Day 0, the patient developed sudden limitation of movement of the right upper extremity and presented to a local municipal hospital, where she was diagnosed with acute cerebral infarction. After emergency "percutaneous intracranial arterial thrombectomy," the limb dysfunction symptoms resolved. During hospitalization, echocardiography showed: 1. right heart enlargement; 2. severe tricuspid regurgitation; 3. pulmonary hypertension (approximately 72 mmHg); 4. central atrial septal defect (patent foramen ovale type); 5. reduced left ventricular diastolic function. She underwent "percutaneous patent foramen ovale closure" and was discharged on oral anticoagulant and lipid-lowering medications. After the procedure, chest tightness developed and progressively worsened. She developed dyspnea after walking a little more on level ground, which was relieved after resting for several minutes, without cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, chest pain, palpitations, nausea, poor appetite, diaphoresis, or other discomfort. Half a year earlier, in approximately 7 months before Day 0, dyspnea worsened, accompanied by right upper extremity pain. She presented to the Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery of a local hospital. Ultrasound indicated right upper extremity venous thrombosis formation and elevated pulmonary artery systolic pressure. She was treated with "rivaroxaban" anticoagulation, cardiotonic therapy, diuresis, and other management; her symptoms improved slightly and she was discharged. More than 2 months earlier, in approximately 2 months before Day 0, her dyspnea worsened again, and she was only able to perform simple daily activities such as getting out of bed, accompanied by intermittent bilateral lower extremity edema. She presented to our hospital's Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery. Right heart catheterization showed mPAP 53/17(31) mmHg, PAWP 4 mmHg, SvO2 55%. She was treated with "ambrisentan + tadalafil" for reduction of pulmonary artery pressure, as well as diuretic and anticoagulation therapy, and she subjectively noted slight improvement in dyspnea. Three days before admission, chest tightness worsened without obvious precipitating cause; she was unable to lie flat and was relieved by sitting up, accompanied by fatigue, poor appetite, and bilateral lower extremity edema, without chest pain, dizziness, headache, or other special discomfort. She presented to our hospital's Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery and received "treprostinil + ambrisentan + tadalafil" for reduction of pulmonary artery pressure, "levosimendan" to improve right heart failure, plus diuretic, anticoagulation, and lipid-lowering therapy, but symptoms did not improve significantly, and she was transferred to our center for further diagnosis and treatment. On review of history, on Day -339, the patient underwent "cerebral angiography + percutaneous intracranial arterial thrombectomy" at a local municipal hospital for acute cerebral infarction, with no residual limb motor dysfunction after the procedure. On Day -323, she underwent "percutaneous patent foramen ovale closure" at the local municipal hospital. She denied a history of hypertension and diabetes; denied a history of hepatitis, TB, or malaria; denied trauma or blood transfusion history; had no history of food or drug allergy; vaccination history followed the routine social immunization program. The patient married at appropriate age; menstrual cycles were regular, with moderate menstrual volume; gravida 1, para 1, with no history of spontaneous abortion. Personal history and family history were unremarkable. Physical examination: temperature 36.6℃, pulse 87/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 86/55 mmHg, height 155 cm, weight 61.0 kg. Appeared anemic. On auscultation, P2 > A2. Breath sounds were clear in both lungs, with no dry or wet rales. Mild bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. Laboratory tests: CBC: WBC 4.74×10^9/L, RBC 2.69×10^12/L, Hb 52↓g/L, PLT 165×10^9/L, MCV 68.5↓fL, MCH 19.3↓pg, MCHC 283↓g/L. NT-proBNP: 327↑pg/mL. Blood gas (Fi O2 21%): pH 7.51↑, PO2 25↓mmHg, PCO2 53↓mmHg. Coagulation: PT 13.4s, INR 1.23↑, APTT 30.8s, Fib 2.61g/L, TT 17.1s, D-dimer 0.28mg/L. Iron studies: serum iron 43.95↑μmol/L; ferritin, unsaturated iron-binding capacity, and total iron-binding capacity showed no abnormality. Folate: 5.04↓ng/mL. Vitamin B12: 156↓pg/mL. Electrolytes, liver and kidney function, blood lipids, three thyroid function tests, myocardial enzymes, troponin, glycated hemoglobin, ESR, three inflammatory markers, four infectious disease tests, and routine urine and stool tests showed no obvious abnormality. Imaging studies: ECG: low-flat or inverted T waves in leads II, III, aVF, and V1-V6; prolonged QTc (467 ms). Echocardiography: occluder in normal position, no atrial-level shunt; mild to moderate tricuspid insufficiency; pulmonary hypertension (estimated sPAP 85 mmHg, mPAP 26 mmHg); left atrial enlargement; high right atrial value; EF 63%. Venous ultrasound of both lower extremities: bilateral deep venous insufficiency of the lower extremities. Thyroid, hepatobiliary, spleen, pancreas, and urinary system ultrasound showed no obvious abnormality. CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) report: a small amount of faint fluffy opacities in both lungs, inflammation or pulmonary edema to be excluded? Scattered small nodules in both lungs; please correlate clinically. Post-percutaneous patent foramen ovale closure changes; please evaluate in conjunction with the clinical findings. Left pleural effusion.

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH)
supporting_evidence: Progressive dyspnea with definite pulmonary hypertension, consistent with the common presentation of CTEPH
Color Doppler ultrasound in approximately 7 months before Day 0 showed right upper extremity venous thrombosis

In approximately 11 months before Day 0, there was a sudden acute cerebral infarction, and interatrial septal communication was present at that time, suggesting a prior thromboembolic event background.
Right heart catheterization showed precapillary pulmonary hypertension (mPAP 31 mmHg, PAWP 4 mmHg)
The patient has been receiving long-term anticoagulant therapy, suggesting that thrombosis-related issues have already been considered clinically.
opposing_evidence: The CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) report did not describe a definite intraluminal filling defect in the pulmonary arteries or signs of chronic thrombus.
Venous ultrasound of both lower extremities showed only bilateral deep venous insufficiency of the lower extremities, with no evidence of deep venous thrombosis in the lower extremities

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with congenital heart disease / atrial septal communication-associated pulmonary vascular disease (persistent or progressive after closure procedure)
supporting_evidence: Previous echocardiography showed a central atrial septal defect (foramen ovale type) with significant pulmonary hypertension, right heart enlargement, and tricuspid regurgitation.
In approximately 10 months before Day 0, chest tightness developed immediately after percutaneous patent foramen ovale closure and progressively worsened
Significant pulmonary hypertension and evidence of right heart strain are still present: P2 > A2, sPAP 85 mmHg, elevated right atrial value, tricuspid regurgitation
opposing_evidence: Current echocardiography and images indicate the occluder is in normal position, with no atrial-level shunt.
Right heart catheterization PAWP 4 mmHg does not support elevated left heart filling pressure caused solely by a left-to-right shunt
No direct evidence of a clearly large shunt or Eisenmenger manifestations was seen in the provided information.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary hypertension associated with left heart disease/heart failure (predominantly diastolic dysfunction)
supporting_evidence: Prior echocardiography indicated impaired left ventricular diastolic function
This echocardiogram showed left atrial enlargement
Orthopnea, bilateral lower extremity edema, and pleural effusion may be seen clinically in heart failure
opposing_evidence: Right heart catheterization: PAWP 4 mmHg, not supportive of pulmonary hypertension primarily due to elevated left heart filling pressure
Echocardiogram: EF 63%, preserved left ventricular systolic function
Breath sounds were clear bilaterally, with no dry or moist rales.
Pulmonary hypertension and abnormal right heart loading are relatively prominent, more consistent with a precapillary mechanism

differential_diagnoses.name: High-output state due to severe anemia or anemic heart failure, exacerbating preexisting cardiopulmonary symptoms
supporting_evidence: Complete blood count showed Hb 52↓g/L, RBC 2.69×10^12/L, indicating severe anemia
MCV 68.5↓fL, MCH 19.3↓pg, MCHC 283↓g/L, indicating microcytic hypochromic changes
Physical examination shows an anemic appearance, and the clinical manifestations include fatigue, chest tightness after exertion, and dyspnea.
Hypotension (86/55 mmHg) can be affected by severe anemia, further exacerbating tissue hypoxia.
opposing_evidence: Severe pulmonary hypertension, P2 > A2, elevated right atrial value, tricuspid regurgitation, and precapillary pulmonary hypertension on right heart catheterization cannot be explained by anemia alone
No description of typical high-output signs was found in the phase 1 information
In the iron studies, serum iron was 43.95↑ μmol/L, with no evidence suggestive of typical iron deficiency anemia.

stage2_input.text: Careful review of the CTPA: On the lung window, multiple ground-glass opacities and mosaic attenuation are seen, which are manifestations of heterogeneous pulmonary blood perfusion; on the mediastinal window, enlargement of the main pulmonary artery is seen, suggesting elevated pulmonary artery pressure; sparse vascular markings are seen in the right upper and middle lobes, with stenotic and occlusive lesions in multiple pulmonary artery subsegments and branches (most prominent in RA1, RA2, RA3, RA4, RA5, RA10, LA4, and LA5), suggesting chronic pulmonary artery thrombotic changes. On repeat review of the head and neck CTA (including both upper lungs) from the patient's cardiothoracic surgery visit 3 months earlier, multiple stenoses and occlusions were seen in the right upper lobe pulmonary artery and its branches. After 3 months of anticoagulation therapy, there was no significant change compared with the current CTPA. Further pulmonary perfusion scintigraphy showed decreased perfusion/perfusion defects in the right upper lobe, right middle lobe, posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe, and lingular segment of the left upper lobe. Right heart catheterization showed: mPAP 47/16(26) mmHg, CI 3.2L/min/m2, PVR 4.7WU, SvO2: 51.3%. Pulmonary angiography showed: enlargement of the main pulmonary artery; extensive stenotic and occlusive lesions in the bilateral pulmonary arteries and their branches, with poor distal blood flow, most prominent in RA1, RA2, RA3, RA4, RA5, RA10, LA4, LA5, and LA8. Further evaluation for the cause of thrombosis was completed: connective tissue disease panel: ANA 1:100(±), remaining antibodies negative; rheumatoid arthritis antibody panel and ANCA panel: no abnormalities; tumor markers: no abnormalities; PET-CT: no obvious abnormal arterial metabolism, no evidence of tumor. Thrombophilia screening: protein S activity 90.5%, protein C activity 52↓%, antithrombin III 89%, factor V activity 84.6%, factor VIII activity 163.3%, factor XI activity 54.7%, vWF activity 148%. Lupus anticoagulant testing: lupus anticoagulant screening ratio 2.12↑, lupus anticoagulant confirm ratio 1.67↑, lupus anticoagulant normalized ratio 1.27↑ (after correction). Antiphospholipid antibody testing: anticardiolipin IgG antibody 42.1↑ CU, anticardiolipin IgA antibody 31.6↑ CU, anticardiolipin IgM antibody 2.9 CU, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein 1 IgG antibody 6.4 CU, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein 1 IgA antibody 4.0 CU, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein 1 IgM antibody 1.1 CU.

recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has CTEPH and previously had manifestations of decompensated right heart failure. At admission, chest tightness and dyspnea had progressively worsened, the patient was unable to lie flat, and had bilateral lower extremity edema and hypotension, and had already received treprostinil, ambrisentan, tadalafil, levosimendan, and diuretic therapy. Repeat NT-proBNP testing can dynamically assess whether right ventricular wall stress and heart failure burden have improved, helping determine whether the current symptoms are still mainly caused by right ventricular insufficiency. If the level decreases significantly but the patient still has severe dyspnea, this suggests a mismatch between improvement in pulmonary vascular/cardiac function and symptom severity, and further investigation for other causes of dyspnea is needed, such as severe anemia, thereby affecting subsequent treatment priorities and risk assessment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Right heart catheterization showed mPAP 26 mmHg and PVR 4.7 WU
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has confirmed CTEPH. Prior right heart catheterization indicated precapillary pulmonary hypertension. Recently, the patient was hospitalized for worsening chest tightness, dyspnea, and manifestations of right heart failure, and received intensified treatment to lower pulmonary artery pressure and improve right heart function. Right heart catheterization is the gold standard for assessing pulmonary artery pressure, pulmonary vascular resistance, cardiac output, and pre- versus postcapillary mechanisms. It can determine whether hemodynamics have truly improved after treatment, the current severity of the condition, and whether there is still a significant right heart load. If mPAP and PVR have improved compared with previously but symptoms remain severe, this helps suggest that the dyspnea is not fully explained by pulmonary hypertension itself, thereby prompting consideration of other causes such as anemia, and also provides a basis for subsequent BPA timing, perioperative risk, and adjustment of the medication regimen.

The patient’s dyspnea has worsened markedly over the past 2 months, and the patient is able to perform only simple activities of daily living. It further deteriorated 3 days before admission, with clinical WHO functional class III-IV. The 6-minute walk test can objectively quantify exercise tolerance and the degree of functional limitation, and is an important tool for risk stratification and treatment response assessment in pulmonary hypertension/CTEPH. In conjunction with the right heart catheterization and NT-proBNP results, if the 6MWD is significantly decreased while hemodynamic improvement is limited yet insufficient to explain such severe activity limitation, this suggests that other factors are still affecting exercise tolerance, such as severely reduced oxygen-carrying capacity due to severe anemia. This test helps determine the authenticity and severity of symptoms and guides whether further correction of anemia is needed and assessment of subsequent treatment response.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Complete blood count suggested microcytic hypochromic anemia
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: In addition to the marked decrease in Hb, the patient also requires a complete blood count to evaluate multiple cell lines such as RBC, WBC, and PLT, in order to determine whether there is isolated erythroid involvement or whether bone marrow suppression, bleeding loss, or other hematologic problems are present. In this case, given long-term anticoagulation, multiple thrombotic events, and severe cardiopulmonary disease, any concomitant platelet abnormality would affect assessment of bleeding/thrombotic risk and the safety of subsequent treatment. Morphologic clues on the complete blood count have already suggested microcytic hypochromic anemia, which is critical for the preliminary differential diagnosis among iron deficiency anemia, anemia of chronic disease, drug-related anemia, and other hematologic disorders, and can also provide a basis for subsequent addition of RBC indices, reticulocyte, and iron studies results.

The patient has severe anemia of unclear etiology, and the severity of dyspnea does not fully correspond to the improvement in pulmonary artery pressure, so further evaluation should begin with anemia classification. Red blood cell indices can determine whether there are microcytic hypochromic changes and help distinguish iron deficiency anemia, anemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic anemia, thalassemia, and some drug-related anemia patterns. In conjunction with the case findings of slightly elevated serum iron, elevated ferritin, normal CRP, and no clear evidence of blood loss, abnormal red blood cell indices may suggest that common iron deficiency anemia is not typical, prompting further investigation for nonclassical causes, including ambrisentan-related adverse reactions, thereby affecting the diagnostic direction and the decision to discontinue the drug.

In the context of the patient having an Hb of 52 g/L and showing no significant improvement after transfusion of suspended red blood cells, it is necessary to determine whether the bone marrow has a compensatory response to the anemia. The reticulocyte percentage can reflect the degree of erythropoietic activity and help distinguish decreased bone marrow production from a compensatory state after peripheral destruction/loss. In this case, an increased reticulocyte count suggests that the bone marrow is not completely unresponsive, which is valuable for excluding a pure aplastic anemia-like condition and for assessing whether hemolysis or recent accelerated consumption is present. Combined with the absence of a clear bleeding history, the absence of typical hemolytic manifestations, and the iron metabolism results, this can further narrow the range of causes of anemia and support the assessment of drug-related anemia.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: The patient had no manifestations of hemolytic anemia such as jaundice, changes in urine color, or elevated blood or urine bilirubin.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient's anemia is progressing relatively rapidly, with Hb decreasing by approximately 30 g/L within 2 months. It is necessary to evaluate for hemolytic anemia, an important potential cause of an abrupt worsening of anemia. Although the history lacks typical manifestations such as jaundice and changes in urine color, clinical manifestations alone are insufficient to completely exclude it. Testing urine bilirubin can help, in conjunction with other hemolysis-related clues, determine whether there is evidence of abnormal bilirubin metabolism and hemolysis. If the findings do not support hemolysis, the diagnostic focus can shift to nonhemolytic causes, such as drug-related anemia, abnormal iron utilization, or abnormal bone marrow hematopoiesis, thereby avoiding misdiagnosis and guiding subsequent drug discontinuation and supportive treatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: in conjunction with the patient's slightly elevated serum iron
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has microcytic hypochromic anemia, but the serum iron is not decreased and is instead slightly elevated, which is inconsistent with typical iron deficiency anemia. Rechecking and monitoring the serum iron level can help assess iron metabolism status and determine whether the microcytic hypochromic changes are caused by iron deficiency or whether there is impaired iron utilization, sideroblastic change, or a drug-related effect. In patients with prolonged severe illness, recurrent hospitalizations, and treatment with multiple medications, managing this simply as iron deficiency may delay identification of the true cause. This test can help exclude common differential diagnoses, shift the clinical approach from “iron-loss anemia” to “non-iron-deficiency anemia,” and affect whether to provide iron supplementation and whether to discontinue suspected medications.

Ferritin is an important indicator for assessing iron stores. Although the patient has microcytic hypochromic anemia, the ferritin is elevated rather than decreased, which is inconsistent with typical iron deficiency anemia. In combination with a slightly elevated serum iron level, normal CRP, and no clear evidence of chronic blood loss, ferritin testing helps determine whether body iron stores are adequate, supports exclusion of iron deficiency as the primary cause, and aids in the differential diagnosis of anemia of chronic inflammation, sideroblastic anemia, and other disorders of iron utilization. This result is of important value in correcting an inappropriate treatment direction, avoiding blind iron supplementation, and further considering drug-induced anemia.

The patient has severe anemia, and it is necessary to differentiate whether it is anemia of chronic disease or inflammation-related anemia. CRP can reflect the status of systemic inflammatory activity. In conjunction with the absence of fever or signs of infectious toxemia in the case, although imaging showed a small amount of flocculent opacity, there is no clear evidence of infection, and the infectious disease tests and the three inflammatory markers are overall without significant abnormalities; a normal CRP helps suggest that active inflammation is not the main mechanism causing the anemia. The value of this test in the differential diagnosis lies in combining it with ferritin, serum iron, and other results to exclude anemia of chronic disease, further supporting a focus on drug-related factors and other non-inflammatory causes of anemia.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: In sideroblastic anemia, the peripheral blood red blood cell histogram shows a single peak
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has microcytic hypochromic anemia, but there is insufficient evidence for common iron deficiency and anemia of chronic disease; meanwhile, serum iron and ferritin are not low, so further analysis of the red blood cell volume distribution characteristics is needed to refine the anemia classification. The peripheral blood red blood cell histogram can help determine from the population distribution pattern whether the findings are consistent with special types of anemia such as sideroblastic anemia. In this case, the histogram showed a single peak, which does not support sideroblastic anemia and helps to further exclude this differential diagnosis and narrow the etiologic range. For this case, the role of this test is that when multiple common etiologies are difficult to explain, morphological distribution clues are used to support the final consideration of drug-induced anemia and provide corroborative evidence for the subsequent discontinuation of ambrisentan.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: After treatment with "treprostinil + ambrisentan + tadalafil" to lower pulmonary artery pressure, "levosimendan" to improve right heart failure, and diuresis, NT-proBNP decreased to 327↑pg/mL. Right heart catheterization showed mPAP 26mmHg and PVR 4.7WU; however, the patient still had fairly significant dyspnea, with functional class III-IV (WHO classification), 6MWD: 247 m↓. The severity of the pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance did not match the severity of the dyspnea. By etiology, dyspnea can be classified as pulmonary, cardiac, toxic, hematologic, neuropsychiatric, etc. This patient had no history or signs related to toxic or neuropsychiatric causes, and despite active treatment of pulmonary and cardiac dyspnea, still had unexplained dyspnea. The patient had severe anemia (Hb 52g/L). Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of red blood cells can cause tissue and organ hypoxia, leading to compensatory breathing and increased heart rate, worsening cardiac workload and respiratory muscle fatigue, resulting in exertional dyspnea. At the first visit to the Department of Cardiovascular Surgery of our hospital 3 months earlier, hemoglobin (Hb) was 81g/L; at this admission, Hb was 52g/L, MCV 68.5↓fL, MCH 19.3↓pg, MCHC 283↓g/L, reticulocyte percentage 3.3%↑. After intermittent transfusion of 2 U of suspended red blood cells, hemoglobin improved only slightly (57g/L). The patient had no manifestations of hemolytic anemia such as jaundice, change in urine color, or elevated urine bilirubin. CBC suggested microcytic hypochromic anemia. Considering the patient's slightly elevated serum iron, elevated ferritin, and normal CRP, the diagnostic criteria for iron deficiency anemia and anemia of chronic disease are not currently met; sideroblastic anemia is not currently considered because the peripheral blood red blood cell histogram showed a single peak; thalassemia has geographic distribution and is not currently considered. Compared with the first visit to our hospital, the patient's hemoglobin at this admission had dropped sharply by about 30g/L within 2 months, without manifestations of bleeding during this period such as increased menstruation, melena, hemoptysis, or hematemesis. However, the patient had started additional pulmonary artery pressure-lowering medications 2 months earlier, including ambrisentan. Common adverse reactions of endothelin receptor antagonists (including ambrisentan) include anemia. In this patient, the hemoglobin decreased significantly (decrease of 36%), and common causes of anemia cannot explain it; drug-induced anemia cannot be excluded.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: Drug-induced anemia (caused by ambrisentan), antiphospholipid syndrome, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, status post atrial septal defect repair
diagnostic_basis: Severe anemia (Hb 52 g/L), microcytic hypochromic anemia

Two months earlier, medications to lower pulmonary arterial pressure were added, including ambrisentan; subsequently, hemoglobin decreased sharply by approximately 30 g/L, with no evidence of bleeding during this period.

Common adverse reactions of endothelin receptor antagonists include anemia; after discontinuation of ambrisentan, 2 U of red blood cells were transfused, and the patient's hemoglobin increased rapidly;

CTPA: On the lung window, multiple ground-glass opacities and a mosaic pattern are seen, which are manifestations of heterogeneous pulmonary perfusion; on the mediastinal window, enlargement of the main pulmonary artery is seen, suggesting elevated pulmonary artery pressure; sparse vascular markings are seen in the right upper and middle lobes, and multiple pulmonary artery subsegments and branches (particularly RA1, RA2, RA3, RA4, RA5, RA10, LA4, and LA5) show stenotic and occlusive lesions, suggesting chronic pulmonary arterial thrombotic changes; echocardiography showed: 1. right heart enlargement 2. severe tricuspid regurgitation 3. pulmonary hypertension (approximately 72 mmHg) 4. central atrial septal defect (patent foramen ovale type) 5. impaired left ventricular diastolic function;

Multiple thromboembolic events; lupus anticoagulant testing: lupus anticoagulant screening ratio 2.12↑, lupus anticoagulant confirmatory ratio 1.67↑, lupus anticoagulant normalized ratio 1.27↑ (after correction). Antiphospholipid antibody testing: anticardiolipin IgG antibody 42.1↑ CU, anticardiolipin IgA antibody 31.6↑ CU, anticardiolipin IgM antibody 2.9 CU, anti-β2-glycoprotein 1 IgG antibody 6.4 CU, anti-β2-glycoprotein 1 IgA antibody 4.0 CU, anti-β2-glycoprotein 1 IgM antibody 1.1 CU.

treatment_plan: Glucocorticoid (prednisone 30 mg qd, taper by 5 mg every 2 weeks to 15 mg qd, then maintain at 15 mg qd)
Immunosuppressant (tacrolimus capsules 1 mg bid to maintain blood concentration at 5-10 ng/ml)
Transfused 2 U of packed red blood cells
treatment_response: After discontinuation of ambrisentan and blood transfusion, hemoglobin increased to 91 g/L
After the anemia improved, dyspnea was significantly relieved compared with previously.
Comparison before and after BPA showed marked improvement in pulmonary artery stenosis and occlusion.
Follow-up echocardiography showed that the patient's right heart had decreased to the normal range in size, and tricuspid valve opening was normal.
The patient's symptoms improved significantly, cardiac function: Class I, 6MWD: 432 m, able to engage in normal physical activity
